answer: The registration of title to every land parcel under the Act must be “in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” Applied here, because the parcel is being brought under the title-registration system, its registration of title must follow that cadastral map.

The statute requires the Commissioner of Title Settlement, upon receipt of the certified copies of cadastral maps, to "publish a Notice in the Gazette," and that Notice must call for "any claimants to the land parcel specified in such Notice to submit their claims to him within a prescribed period from the date of publication of such Notice." After claims are made in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement "shall cause an investigation to be conducted in order to determine the genuinness or otherwise of claims made." Applied here, potential claimants must be invited by Gazette notice, and once claims are received, an investigation must be carried out to assess whether the claims are genuine or not.

The provisions create two different procedures.

1. **Reference of disputed claims for investigation and determination**: Under section 21, **if, during the course of investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, due to the disputed nature of the claims, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court**, the Commissioner of Title Settlement **may refer such claims for investigation and determination to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate**. This is a referral made by the Commissioner because the claims are disputed.

2. **Procedure for an aggrieved claimant**: Under section 22, **any claimant aggrieved by any Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14 may prefer an appeal against such declaration within the prescribed period to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate**. This is an appeal by the claimant, and it must be made within the prescribed period.

So, the first procedure is a **Commissioner-initiated referral of disputed claims for investigation and determination**, while the second is a **claimant-initiated appeal against a declaration**, brought within the prescribed period.

The transferee did not acquire the interest on the facts given. Under s 38, “No person acquiring an interest in any land parcel registered under the provisions of this Act shall be entitled to such title or interest unless such title or interest is registered under the provisions of this Act.” Under s 49, “An instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the provisions of this Act shall take effect on registration, of such instrument under the provisions of this Act.” So, for land parcel registered under the Act, the private agreement alone does not make the transferee entitled to the interest; the instrument takes effect only upon registration.

Section 48 provides that, except in accordance with the provisions of the Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under the Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common, “shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.”

Applied to the facts, the registered owner executes one instrument purporting to convey the parcel to two purchasers as owners in common. That is an instrument made in favour of two persons in common, so it is void and not registrable under the Act unless it is in accordance with the provisions of the Act.

The statutory rule is that, for lands or interests in land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, “The Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) shall not apply” and “The Partition Act shall not apply” to land parcels so registered. [node_id: 21-1998/section-57; 21-1998/section-63]

Applied here, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Therefore, the Prescription Ordinance does not apply to a prescription claim over that parcel, and the Partition Act does not apply to a partition action concerning that parcel. [node_id: 21-1998/section-57; 21-1998/section-63]

Rule: Subject to section 60, a Court may order rectification of the Register where it is satisfied that any registration has been obtained by fraud. However, a Court "shall not order the rectification of a register so as to affect the title of a registered owner who is in possession and who has acquired the land parcel or interest therein for valuable consideration, unless such owner was a party to such fraud." [21-1998/section-59, 21-1998/section-59/proviso-1]

Application: The registration was obtained by fraud, so the court would generally have power to rectify. But the present registered owner is in possession, acquired the parcel for valuable consideration, and was not a party to the fraud. Therefore, the court shall not order rectification so as to affect that owner’s title. [21-1998/section-59, 21-1998/section-59/proviso-1]

Indemnity: Section 60 provides indemnity for "not rectifying the Register in consequence of an order of Court made under section 59." On the facts given, the loss arose because the register was not rectified, so the person who suffered loss may claim indemnity on that basis. [21-1998/section-60/subsection-1/paragraph-b]

The statutory steps are as follows.

First, once the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the provisions of the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and this Act, he must certify the plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General, then:
- “file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title”; and
- “forward the duplicate of the condominium plan and the application of the owner to the appropriate Registrar of Title”.

Then the Registrar of Title must:
- “file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File”; and
- “open a new title register in the Register in respect of each condominium parcel shown on the Condominium Plan and make suitable cross references to such register in the register in which the land parcel is registered”.

Applied here, because the plan has been approved as conforming to the applicable laws, the Superintendent may certify it and carry out the filing and forwarding steps above, and the Registrar must then file the duplicate plan and open a new title register for each condominium parcel with the required cross-references.

Statutory rule: Under section 22, when a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, “the surviving spouse shall inherit one-half of the property.” Under section 23, subject to that spouse’s right, inheritance goes first to “(a) descendants.” Under section 24, “Children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent to all others in the estate of the parents; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.”

Application to the facts: The surviving spouse takes 1/2 of the estate first.

The remaining 1/2 passes to descendants. There are two descendant branches: (1) the living child, and (2) the deceased child’s branch represented by the two grandchildren. The living child takes one branch share, and the two grandchildren take the other branch share by representation.

Calculation:
- Total estate = 1
- Spouse = 1/2
- Remaining for descendants = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2
- That remaining 1/2 is divided into 2 branches = 1/2 ÷ 2 = 1/4 per branch
- Living child = 1/4
- Deceased child’s branch = 1/4
- Each grandchild = 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8

Final shares:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: 1/8

The rule is that a will made beyond Sri Lanka that contains a devise or disposition of immovable property situated in Sri Lanka will be “valid and effectual to alienate and pass” that property if it was “duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed” and if it was made by a person who “by the law of such country or of Sri Lanka” was competent to make a will. 

Applied here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it disposes of immovable property in Sri Lanka, it complied with the formalities of the country where it was executed, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. Those facts satisfy the statutory conditions, so the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

The statute provides that, in proceedings or an action for enforcing a right of pre-emption, “No precept or order for the service of notice or summons shall be issued ... until proof is furnished to the court of the registration of the proceedings or action as a lis pendens.” So, before notice or summons is issued, proof of registration of the action as a lis pendens must be furnished to the court.

It also provides that, after the institution of such an action, the court may in its discretion order the plaintiff to deposit “the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5.”

If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period, or further periods not exceeding three months in the aggregate, allowed by the court, “his action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases.”

Applied here: because the plaintiff has not yet proved registration as a lis pendens, notice or summons should not be issued until that proof is furnished. The court may also order the plaintiff to deposit the purchase amount stated in the section 5 notice, and if the plaintiff does not make that deposit within the allowed time, the action must be struck off the roll of pending cases.

The governing rule is that “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.” Here, after the appointed day, the owner of a tea estate mortgages a physically divided portion of that estate as a separate lot. That is a mortgage of a part of a tea estate as a divided lot, so the mortgage is null and void.

The statutory rule is that “[n]o share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property.” So the share in the common elements cannot be disposed of separately while retaining the condominium parcel.

The same provision also says that “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel notwithstanding the fact that no specific or particular reference has been made thereto in the instrument or deed relating to such alienation.” So when the condominium parcel is transferred, the accompanying share in the common elements is transferred with it, even if the deed does not specifically mention that share.

The statutory rule is that “The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.” [11-1973/section-23]

Applied to the facts, the property in question is “land and a building already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan.” Because it falls within that description, the Partition Law does not apply to it. [11-1973/section-23]

Under section 13, a plan or map, or copy or tracing of it, is not receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless it has been prepared in one of the forms stated in the section. The supplied text states two relevant forms:

- paragraph (a): it must be prepared "by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him" and certified "by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for such purpose"; or
- paragraph (b): it must be "and certified by a registered licensed surveyor."

So, before it can be received in evidence, the plan or map must satisfy the preparation and certification wording set out in section 13.

Yes. Under the provision, any cadastral map or plan that is a copy “purporting to be a true copy” and “purporting to be signed by the surveyor general or any officer acting on his behalf” “shall be admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It also “may be taken as prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original.” Applying that rule here, the copy purporting to be authenticated and signed by the Surveyor-General is admissible in place of the original, and it initially receives prima facie evidential status as to the truth of the facts stated in it, until evidence to the contrary is given. Also, it is not necessary to prove that the copy was in fact signed or authenticated, or that it is a true copy.

The rule is that, “Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the articles of a company, it shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares in or debentures of the company, unless a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company.” So, on the facts given, the company may not register the voluntary transfer because no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered. 

The exception is that “nothing in this section shall affect any power of the company to register as shareholder or debenture holder, any person to whom the right of any shares in or debentures of the company has been transmitted by operation of law.” So where entitlement passes by operation of law, the company’s power to register that person is not affected by this section.

Under Companies Act, s 79, “A certificate signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company specifying any shares held by any shareholder, shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares.”

Applied here, a share certificate signed in the company’s name by a director and the secretary, and specifying the shares held by the shareholder, is prima facie evidence that the recorded shareholder has title to those shares.

The director breached these statutory duties:

1. Duty to comply with the company’s articles: a director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes ... the provisions contained in the articles of the company.” Because the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, this duty is breached. [node_id: 7-2007/section-188]

2. Duty not to act recklessly or grossly negligently: a director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.” Because the director carried out the decision recklessly, this duty is breached. [node_id: 7-2007/section-189/paragraph-a]

3. Duty to exercise the required skill and care: a director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.” Because the director did not exercise the skill and care reasonably expected from a person with that director’s knowledge and experience, this duty is breached. [node_id: 7-2007/section-189/paragraph-b]

The statutory rule is that “Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law.” Applying that rule here, because the transfer of land was completed in direct contravention of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, the alienation is void and has no effect in law.
